newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. official hits EU over phone callback tax.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official hits EU over phone callback tax.

text.p: U.S. Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt said on Sunday a European Union plan to tax phone callback services ran against efforts to free global telecommunications and bring down prices.

He told Reuters in an interview that although he was hopeful a telecoms pact between some 60 countries could be completed in World Trade Organisation talks by the February 15 deadline there were still "serious problems" to resolve.

"High tariffs and high taxes are mutually problematic," he said in a comment on the EU plan which would aim to compel callback operators, mainly U.S.-based, to pay value-added tax on services to clients in Europe.

"The notion that you would break up the super-tariff system and try to move to competitive prices only to replace those tariffs with super-taxes is really a fine way to defeat the whole purpose of the (WTO) negotiations," Hundt added.

Callback systems allow telephone users in Europe and other countries with high international rates to save up to 70 per cent on their costs by routing calls through the United States, where charges are much lower.
The measure, proposed by the European Commission last week after pressure from EU member governments, has yet to be formally approved and would not go into effect until 1999.
It would also provide for VAT, ranging from 15 to 25 per cent among the 15 states of the EU, to be charged on calls made using telephone cards issued by non-European companies.
Hundt, speaking in Davos where he is attending the World Economic Forum of political and business leaders, said callback systems were "a way round the cartel....
"People will find a way round fundamentally unfair and economically irrational pricing systems.

"When they are finding ways around those obstacles to trade, the right reaction is to rationalise the trading system, not to try to tax the pressure valves," said the FCC chief, effectively U.S. communications minister.
The EU has not yet spelt out how it would collect the tax, levying which would involve asking callback companies outside Brussels' jurisdiction to provide details of their business.
U.S.-based callback companies, and some officials, have questioned whether the idea is practical.

Hundt, who will join the U.S. team in Geneva for the final two or three days of the WTO telecom talks, said if Malaysia made an offer as promised within the next few days it could have a significant effect.

Malaysia, a key emerging economy, is one of the holdouts in the negotiations aimed at opening up the $600 billion sector to international competition, and Hundt said its stance could be important "for all of South-East Asia."

But he said problems still to be resolved included an apparent EU aim to exclude from a pact transmission of any data that could be received in video form and Canada's insistence on restricting foreign ownership of telecoms firms to 46 per cent.

Hundt said the United States, which walked away from earlier talks due to have been concluded last April saying insufficient quality offers were on the table to justify throwing open the U.S. market, would not negotiate beyond the deadline.

"Everyone knows what they have to do for an agreement to be possible," he said. The United States is considered vital for a pact because it has some 50 per cent of the entire world basic telecoms market.
